text: You already know a single ACL can combine a role, a condition, and a script, all of them required together. This lesson goes deeper into how to write the script half of that combination well -- because ACL scripts carry a performance risk most other scripts don't.

A slow business rule slows down one transaction. A slow ACL script is worse, because ACL scripts run on every single access attempt to the record or field they govern -- every form load, every list view that includes the field, every Table API call, every report. Fifty extra milliseconds becomes fifty milliseconds multiplied across every user, every record, all day long.

The single most common mistake is running a fresh GlideRecord query inside an ACL script to answer a question the platform can already answer more cheaply. Here, the script queries sys_user_grmember directly to check whether the current user belongs to a given group. It works, but it issues a real database query every single time the ACL runs, for every record, every field, every user.

GlideUser, returned by gs.getUser(), already holds the current user's roles and group memberships for the transaction, loaded once and reused. Its isMemberOf method answers the exact same question as that query, without issuing one. This is the real, standard pattern for 'only members of this group can access this record' -- same result, no per-access database round trip.

The same principle extends past group membership. If the information you need is already sitting on current, the record being evaluated, use it directly instead of querying somewhere else to re-derive it. A direct field comparison is effectively free compared to a query. The general rule: keep ACL scripts fast and simple, and reach for a query only when there's genuinely no cheaper way to get the answer.
Fast scripts, cached data, queries as a last resort. Next up: field-level security design patterns, for protecting one sensitive field without breaking access to the rest of the record.
